newsitem.title: USA: Brazil credit curbs not best medicine - US analysts.
newsitem.headline: Brazil credit curbs not best medicine - US analysts.

text.p: Brazil's credit curbs enacted Friday sparked concern among U.S. analysts, who said the measures could shave some of the recent gains from the nation's Brady debt.

Brazil raised taxes on credit transactions by individuals in an attempt to curb purchases of durable goods, which have contributed to the country's growing trade gap, Central Bank President Gustavo Loyola said at a news conference.
Earlier, Brazil posted a $951 million trade deficit for April, well above market expectations of a $700 million to $800 million gap.

"I think it's a second-best policy," Paulo Leme, senior international economist at Goldman Sachs, said of the credit hike. "The best policy really is faster fiscal adjustment, but I think it's the right immediate-run response."
While the tax measures should help the trade balance somewhat, an interest-rate hike should also be enacted, Leme said.
"I would venture that within the next month or, that would be a consideration -- I don't think immediately, not next week," he said.
Marcelo Fleury, head of the Brazil Desk at Garban Corp, said the tax increase "is a bitter medicine."
"The ballooning trade deficit has caused concerns in the government, but doubling the consumption tax is bound to be unpopular and may affect the GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth," he said.
Fleury called the move "overdue," as many analysts had expected it would be announced at last week's National Monetary Council meeting.
"Tighter credit and the April trade figure would put pressure on the debt paper next week," Fleury said.
